chapter: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
subject: General
text: In science, a simplified representation of a real system that focuses only on what matters for a given question is called a:
explanation: A model is a simplified way of looking at a real system, deliberately ignoring unimportant details (e.g. treating a falling object as a point mass while ignoring air resistance).

chapter: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
subject: General
text: Which statement best distinguishes a scientific law from a scientific theory?
options: A law is only a guess, while a theory is proven fact
A law describes a regular observed pattern, while a theory explains why that pattern occurs
A theory is less reliable than a law
A law and a theory mean exactly the same thing
explanation: A law describes a pattern (e.g. Newton's laws describing the jerk felt when a bus stops), while a theory goes further and explains why the pattern occurs, based on evidence (e.g. atomic theory explaining how molecules form).

chapter: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
subject: General
text: Meghnad Saha explained the colour of stars by treating the star's matter as a hot gas and ignoring many complex internal processes. This is an example of:
explanation: Saha simplified the star to a hot gas and focused only on temperature, pressure and ion formation — exactly how models are built in science, by ignoring details not relevant to the question.

chapter: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
subject: General
text: A reasoned expectation about what will happen, based on evidence and careful thinking, is called a:
explanation: A scientific prediction is a reasoned expectation based on evidence, not a guess; when predictions do not match observations, scientists re-examine their models or assumptions.

chapter: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
subject: General
text: Why are standard (SI) units used everywhere in science rather than local or informal units?
options: They allow measurements to be compared and results reproduced consistently across the world
They make calculations always give whole numbers
explanation: SI units are based on agreed international standards, so results can be compared and errors (like the aircraft fuel miscalculation from mixing pounds and kilograms) are avoided.

chapter: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
subject: General
text: Which of these is an example of a scientific principle, as distinguished from a law?
options: Newton's laws explaining a jerk when a bus stops
The conservation of energy applied while climbing stairs
The atomic theory of molecule formation
A rough estimate of air breathed per day
explanation: Principles are broad ideas applied to make sense of a situation; the conservation of energy used while climbing stairs is given in the chapter as an example of a principle.

chapter: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
subject: General
text: Robert Hooke-style careful testing shows that scientific theories:
options: are open to improvement and can change as new evidence appears
must always be proved using mathematics only
explanation: The chapter stresses that no scientific theory is ever final; ideas are revised as new evidence becomes available — this openness to correction is a strength of science.

chapter: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
subject: General
text: An approximate estimate (rather than an exact value) is most useful when:
options: checking whether a result is reasonable, without needing exact precision
measuring exact distances for a satellite launch
none of these situations need any estimation
explanation: The chapter's rice/air-breathing examples show estimation is useful to judge if an answer is roughly sensible, even though it is not exact.

chapter: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
subject: General
text: Two students disagree about whether 'clouds look dark, so it will rain' is a scientific prediction. What makes a claim scientifically testable?
options: It only needs to match someone's gut feeling
It must be based on measurable evidence and checkable past patterns
It must always be stated by a scientist
explanation: Meghna's questions about humidity, wind and past rain patterns show that a scientifically testable prediction relies on measurable data and comparison with past patterns, not vague impressions.

chapter: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
subject: General
text: Why does science divide study into separate branches like physics, chemistry and biology, even though nature itself has no such boundaries?
options: To make certain branches more important than others
Purely for convenience and organisation of knowledge, since real problems usually need several branches together
Because each branch uses a completely different universe's rules
Because only physics is a true science
explanation: The chapter explicitly says these divisions are made only to help organise knowledge and are not independent of each other — real problems like understanding a mask need physics, chemistry and biology together.

chapter: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
subject: General
text: A claim on social media says eating food is harmful during a solar eclipse. How would a scientific thinker evaluate this claim?
options: Believe it because many people say so
Ask whether any physical, chemical or biological mechanism actually supports the claim, using evidence
Avoid eating during every eclipse just to be safe
Reject it only because it was shared online
explanation: The chapter's example concludes that no physical, chemical or biological mechanism supports the claim — evidence-based questioning, not belief or blind rejection, is the scientific approach.

chapter: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
subject: General
text: Quantities such as mass, velocity, force and electric current are represented in science using:
options: symbols (such as m, v, F, I) each with a defined unit
random letters chosen for convenience with no fixed meaning
explanation: Science uses a shared language of specific symbols and units (m, v, F, I, etc.) so that results can be communicated clearly and unambiguously across the world.

chapter: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
subject: General
text: Mathematics in science is best described as:
options: a hurdle meant to make science difficult
a language that helps express and test relationships between quantities clearly
unnecessary for understanding motion or reactions
explanation: The chapter explains that mathematics is a language for reasoning about relationships (e.g. between distance, time and velocity), not just a tool for memorised calculation.

chapter: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
subject: General
text: A scientific theory is best failed/falsified when:
options: a new prediction from it does not match a careful observation, based on evidence, not opinion
it was proposed a long time ago
explanation: The chapter states that scientists reject or revise ideas only based on evidence when predictions do not match observations — never based on opinion or belief.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
subject: Biology
text: According to the Cell Theory, new cells are formed:
options: only inside the nucleus of another cell
explanation: Rudolf Virchow expanded the Cell Theory to state that new cells are formed only from pre-existing cells, through cell division.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
subject: Biology
text: Which scientist first reported that all plants are made up of cells?
explanation: Matthias Schleiden (1838), a German botanist, reported that all plants are made of cells; Schwann extended this to animals a year later.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
subject: Biology
text: A cell that lacks a well-defined, membrane-bound nucleus is called a:
explanation: Prokaryotic cells (e.g. bacteria) lack a membrane-bound nucleus; their genetic material lies in a region called the nucleoid.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
subject: Biology
text: The movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane, from a region of higher water concentration to lower, is called:
explanation: Osmosis is specifically the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane; diffusion more generally is net movement of particles from higher to lower concentration, with or without a membrane.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
subject: Biology
text: In the potato-piece experiment, the piece placed in a 20% salt solution shrinks because:
options: salt molecules enter the cells through the membrane
the solution is hypertonic, so water moves out of the cells by osmosis
the cell wall dissolves in salt
explanation: A concentrated (hypertonic) external solution has less water and more solute than the cell interior, so water leaves the cells by osmosis, causing them to shrink.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
subject: Biology
text: Which organelle is correctly described as 'the powerhouse of the cell' and why?
options: Mitochondria — its folded inner membrane (cristae) increases surface area for cellular respiration, releasing energy as ATP
explanation: Mitochondria release energy from glucose breakdown during cellular respiration; the cristae increase surface area for these reactions, and the energy is stored as ATP.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
subject: Biology
text: Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum (RER) differs from Smooth ER (SER) because RER:
options: has ribosomes attached and is mainly involved in protein synthesis/secretion
explanation: RER has ribosomes on its surface (giving it a rough appearance) and is involved in protein synthesis and secretion, e.g. in pancreatic gland cells; SER lacks ribosomes and is involved in lipid/hormone synthesis and storage.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
subject: Biology
text: Which plant organelle is responsible for carrying out photosynthesis?
explanation: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, the green pigment that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis; the sugars formed are stored in the stroma.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
subject: Biology
text: Plastids that store starch, oils or proteins but contain no pigment (e.g. in potato cells) are called:
explanation: Leucoplasts (Greek leukos = white) are colourless plastids specialised for storing food material such as starch, oils or proteins.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
subject: Biology
text: Mitosis and meiosis differ mainly in that:
options: mitosis produces 4 daughter cells with full chromosome number, meiosis produces 2 with half
mitosis produces 2 genetically identical daughter cells with the full chromosome number; meiosis produces 4 daughter cells with half the chromosome number, for gamete formation
both occur only in reproductive organs
both always produce genetically identical cells
explanation: Mitosis makes two identical daughter cells (for growth/repair), while meiosis involves two successive divisions producing four gametes, each with half the parent's chromosome number.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
subject: Biology
text: Why do mature human Red Blood Cells (RBCs) lack a nucleus?
options: To allow more space for haemoglobin so they can carry more oxygen
Because they never need to be replaced
Because they do not contain cytoplasm
explanation: The absence of a nucleus provides more internal space for haemoglobin, letting RBCs carry a larger amount of oxygen; however, they also cannot repair or divide, limiting their lifespan to about 120 days.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
subject: Biology
text: Cell division that goes uncontrolled, losing the normal 'contact inhibition' that stops animal cells from dividing further, can lead to the formation of:
explanation: When cells lose contact inhibition and keep dividing uncontrollably, the result is abnormal growths called tumours — a hallmark of cancer cells.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
subject: Biology
text: The 'fluid-mosaic model' describes the structure of the:
explanation: The fluid-mosaic model explains the cell membrane as a lipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it like tiles in a mosaic, with molecules free to move sideways within the fluid membrane.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
subject: Biology
text: J. Craig Venter's 2010 synthetic-biology experiment, in which synthetic DNA was inserted into an existing bacterial cell (with its DNA removed), demonstrated that:
options: an entirely new cell can be built from non-living chemicals alone
DNA controls the structure and activities of a cell
mitochondria are not needed for cell function
plant cells and animal cells are identical
explanation: The experiment showed that once synthetic DNA was inserted into an existing cell (whose own DNA was removed), the cell followed the new DNA's instructions to grow and divide — demonstrating that DNA controls a cell's structure and activity; the rest of the cell was not newly created.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
subject: Biology
text: Which structure allows transfer of material between the nucleus and the cytoplasm?
options: Nuclear pores in the nuclear membrane
explanation: The double-layered nuclear membrane has pores (nuclear pores) that allow material, such as ribosomal subunits, to pass between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
subject: Biology
text: A large central vacuole in a mature plant cell mainly helps by:
options: storing water, minerals and waste, maintaining pressure that keeps the cell firm
explanation: The vacuole, filled with cell sap, stores water/minerals/waste and maintains internal pressure (turgor); when water is lost, the vacuole shrinks and the plant wilts.

chapter: Cell: The Building Block of Life
subject: Biology
text: Totipotency, demonstrated by Gottlieb Haberlandt's idea and later used in plant tissue culture, refers to the ability of a cell to:
options: develop into a complete new organism given the right conditions
explanation: Totipotency is the special ability of a plant cell — even a mature one — to develop into a complete plant when given suitable nutrients and conditions, the basis of plant tissue culture.

subject: Biology
text: A group of similar cells performing the same function together is called a:
explanation: A tissue is defined as a group of cells, similar in structure, that work together to perform a specific function.

subject: Biology
text: Which meristematic tissue is responsible for an increase in the length of roots and shoots?
explanation: Apical meristem, located at root and shoot tips, consists of actively dividing cells that make roots and shoots grow in length (demonstrated by the onion root-tip experiment).

subject: Biology
text: Grass regrowing quickly after mowing is explained by the activity of the:
explanation: Intercalary meristem, located at the base of internodes/nodes in plants like grasses, allows regeneration after the tip is cut or grazed.

subject: Biology
text: Which simple permanent tissue consists of living, loosely packed cells with thin walls and mainly stores food or carries out photosynthesis?
explanation: Parenchyma cells are living, thin-walled and loosely packed with intercellular spaces; besides storage, chlorophyll-containing parenchyma photosynthesises in green plant parts.

subject: Biology
text: Sclerenchyma tissue is hard and strong mainly because of the deposition of:
explanation: Sclerenchyma cells have thick walls due to lignin deposition, making the tissue hard and strong — found in coconut husk and walnut shells, for example.

subject: Biology
text: Xylem is the plant tissue mainly responsible for transporting:
options: food from leaves to other parts
water and minerals from roots to other parts, and providing strength
explanation: Xylem transports water and minerals upward from the roots and also provides mechanical strength to the plant.

subject: Biology
text: Which cells regulate the loading and unloading of sugars in sieve tubes of the phloem?
explanation: Companion cells are specialised parenchyma cells whose main function is to monitor and regulate the movement of sugars into and out of the sieve tubes.

subject: Biology
text: Epithelial tissue lining the small intestine, specialised for efficient absorption, is typically made of:
options: a single layer of tall, pillar-like cells, often with hair-like structures
explanation: Absorptive epithelium (e.g. in the small intestine) is a single layer of tall, columnar cells, sometimes with hair-like projections, to maximise uptake of nutrients and water.

subject: Biology
text: Blood and bone are both classified as connective tissue mainly because:
options: they are both hard and solid
both connect/support other tissues, differing in the consistency of their matrix (fluid vs solid)
explanation: Both blood (fluid matrix) and bone (hard, solid matrix) perform a connecting/supporting role, which is why both are classed as connective tissue despite very different consistency.

subject: Biology
text: Which connective tissue connects muscle to bone, enabling movement?
explanation: Tendons connect muscles to bones; when a muscle contracts, the tendon transmits the force to the bone, producing movement at a joint.

subject: Biology
text: Cardiac muscle differs from skeletal muscle in that cardiac muscle:
options: is involuntary, with branched fibres and a single nucleus, allowing tireless rhythmic contraction
has multiple nuclei per cell and no striations
is found in the stomach and intestine
explanation: Cardiac muscle fibres are cylindrical, branched, have a single nucleus and faint striations, letting the heart beat rhythmically and tirelessly without conscious control.

subject: Biology
text: Smooth muscle, found in organs like the stomach and intestine, is responsible for:
options: slow, continuous involuntary movements such as digestion
explanation: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped, unstriated and under involuntary control, producing slow continuous movements such as peristalsis during digestion.

subject: Biology
text: The part of a neuron that receives signals from other neurons is the:
explanation: Dendrites receive incoming signals from other neurons, while the axon carries the outgoing message away from the cell body to the axon terminals.

subject: Biology
text: Which type of joint allows the shoulder to move forward, backward, sideways and in a circular motion?
explanation: The ball and socket joint of the shoulder, where the rounded head of the upper arm bone fits into a shallow socket, permits the widest range of movement.

subject: Biology
text: The elbow and knee, which can only bend and straighten in one direction (like a door), contain a:
explanation: A hinge joint, as in the elbow and knee, permits movement in only one plane, similar to the hinge of a door.

subject: Biology
text: The skull bones are joined by fixed joints mainly to:
options: allow maximum rotation of the head
keep the brain protected and safe by preventing movement between skull bones
explanation: Fixed joints hold the skull bones firmly together so that they cannot move relative to each other, keeping the delicate brain safe even during body movement.

subject: Biology
text: A plant's stem bends in strong wind without breaking because of flexible collenchyma tissue, whereas a woody trunk relies more on rigid sclerenchyma. This difference illustrates that:
options: all simple permanent tissues behave identically
tissue structure (thin, pectin-rich walls vs thick, lignified walls) is matched to the mechanical function required
sclerenchyma is always more flexible than collenchyma
plants have no supporting tissue at all
explanation: Collenchyma's thin, unevenly thickened (pectin) walls give flexibility (bending without breaking), while sclerenchyma's thick, lignified walls give rigidity and strength — each tissue's structure suits a different mechanical need.

subject: Physics
text: Displacement is defined as:
options: the total path length covered by a moving object
the net change in position of an object between two instants of time
the time taken to complete a journey
always equal to the distance travelled
explanation: Displacement is the net (straight-line) change in position between the start and end points, which can be smaller than (or equal to, but never greater than) the distance travelled.

subject: Physics
text: A person walks 250 m from home to a shop, returns home, then walks 250 m to the shop again. What is the total distance travelled and the net displacement for this whole trip (ending at the shop)?
explanation: Distance = 250 + 250 + 250 = 750 m (there and back and there again); displacement is measured from the start (home) to the final position (shop) = 250 m.

subject: Physics
text: The average speed of an object is calculated as:
options: total distance travelled divided by the time taken
change in velocity divided by time
explanation: Average speed = total distance travelled ÷ time taken, using the total path length (unlike average velocity, which uses displacement).

subject: Physics
text: A car starts from rest and reaches a velocity of 24 m/s in 6 s with constant acceleration. What is its average acceleration and the distance travelled in those 6 s?
explanation: a = (v−u)/t = (24−0)/6 = 4 m/s². Distance s = ut + ½at² = 0 + ½(4)(36) = 72 m.

subject: Physics
text: A motorbike moving at 28 m/s with constant (negative) acceleration stops after travelling 98 m. What is its acceleration?

subject: Physics
text: If an object moves in a circular path at constant speed, its velocity:
options: remains constant in both magnitude and direction
keeps changing direction, so this motion is still accelerated (uniform circular motion)
explanation: In uniform circular motion, speed stays constant but direction continuously changes, so velocity (a vector) changes — meaning the object is accelerating even though its speed is constant.

subject: Physics
text: Which of these kinematic quantities is a vector (has direction), unlike the others?
explanation: Displacement is a vector quantity (it has both magnitude and direction), while distance, speed and time are scalar quantities.

subject: Physics
text: A truck driver slows down from 54 km/h to 36 km/h in 36 s with constant acceleration. What distance is covered in this time? (Convert to m/s: 54 km/h = 15 m/s, 36 km/h = 10 m/s)
explanation: Average velocity = (15+10)/2 = 12.5 m/s; distance = average velocity × time = 12.5 × 36 = 450 m.

subject: Physics
text: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 5 s, travels at 20 m/s for 10 s, then brakes uniformly to stop in 6 s. What is the total distance travelled?

subject: Chemistry
text: Which of these is a heterogeneous mixture?
explanation: Milk is a heterogeneous mixture (a colloid) — its composition is not completely uniform throughout, unlike true solutions such as sugar solution, air or vinegar.

subject: Chemistry
text: The scattering of light by dispersed particles, seen in colloids and suspensions but not true solutions, is called the:
explanation: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by particles of colloidal/suspension size (1 nm–1000 nm and above); true solution particles are too small to scatter light this way.

subject: Chemistry
text: Distillation is most suitable for separating:
options: two immiscible liquids of different densities
two miscible liquids with a boiling-point difference of at least about 25°C
a solid dissolved in a liquid to recover the solid by crystallisation only
a mixture of two solids with similar solubility
explanation: Distillation separates miscible liquids with a reasonable difference in boiling points (the chapter specifies a minimum difference of about 25°C) by selectively vaporising and condensing the lower-boiling liquid first.

subject: Chemistry
text: A separating funnel is used to separate:
options: two immiscible liquids of different densities, such as oil and water
a solid dissolved in a liquid
explanation: A separating funnel exploits the difference in density between two immiscible liquids (e.g. oil and water), which form separate layers that can be drained off one at a time.

subject: Chemistry
text: The direct change of a solid into vapour (without passing through the liquid state) is called:
explanation: Sublimation is the transition of a solid directly to vapour; the reverse process (vapour directly to solid) is called deposition.

subject: Chemistry
text: Centrifugation is commonly used to:
options: separate two miscible liquids by boiling point
rapidly spin a mixture to separate heavier solid particles from a liquid
change a solid directly to a gas
measure the concentration of a solution
explanation: Centrifugation uses rapid spinning to quickly separate denser solid particles from a liquid, faster than ordinary settling or filtration.

subject: Chemistry
text: A brass alloy contains 70% copper by mass. How much copper and zinc are present in 120 g of this brass?
explanation: Copper = 70% of 120 g = 0.70 × 120 = 84 g; zinc (the remaining mass) = 120 − 84 = 36 g.

subject: Chemistry
text: Paper chromatography separates the components of a mixture mainly based on differences in their:
options: rates of movement (solubility/adsorption) on the paper
explanation: Paper chromatography separates substances (e.g. pigments) based on how differently they move/spread on the paper due to differing solubility and adsorption.

subject: Chemistry
text: A colloid differs from a true solution mainly because a colloid's dispersed particles:
options: are smaller than 1 nm and settle quickly
are of intermediate size (roughly 1–1000 nm), do not settle on standing, and scatter light
can always be seen with the naked eye
explanation: Colloidal particles are intermediate in size between true-solution particles and suspension particles; they remain dispersed (don't settle) and scatter light, showing the Tyndall effect.

subject: Physics
text: Newton's First Law of Motion states that an object will remain at rest or move with constant velocity unless:
options: a net external force acts on it
explanation: Newton's First Law (law of inertia) states that an object continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted upon by a net external force.

subject: Physics
text: According to Newton's Second Law, the acceleration produced by a net force on an object is:
options: directly proportional to the force and inversely proportional to the object's mass
inversely proportional to the force and directly proportional to the mass
independent of both force and mass
explanation: Newton's Second Law: a = F/m, so acceleration increases with greater net force and decreases with greater mass, for the same force.

subject: Physics
text: Newton's Third Law of Motion states that:
options: every action has an equal and opposite reaction force on the other object, acting simultaneously
forces always act only in one direction
mass and weight are the same thing
objects at rest exert no force at all
explanation: For every force one object exerts on a second object, the second object simultaneously exerts an equal and opposite force back on the first — action and reaction pairs act on different objects at the same time.

subject: Physics
text: A table is pushed with a constant horizontal force F and moves at constant velocity across the floor. What is the frictional force exerted by the floor?
options: Equal in magnitude to F, opposing the motion
Less than F but in the same direction as the motion
explanation: Constant velocity means zero net force (Newton's First Law), so the frictional force must exactly balance the applied force F in the opposite direction.

subject: Physics
text: 100 oarsmen row a boat; 95 row to propel it forward and (by mistake) 5 row in the opposite direction, each applying 200 N. What is the net force on the boat (ignoring drag)?
explanation: Net force = (95 − 5) × 200 N = 90 × 200 = 18,000 N in the direction the majority (95 oarsmen) are rowing.

subject: Physics
text: When a sailor jumps forward out of a small, initially stationary boat onto the shore, the boat:
options: moves backward, away from the shore, by Newton's third law
explanation: As the sailor pushes backward against the boat to jump forward, the boat experiences an equal and opposite reaction force pushing it backward, away from the shore.

subject: Physics
text: A 50 g bullet moving at 100 m/s enters a wooden block and stops after penetrating 50 cm, with constant deceleration. What is the stopping force on the bullet?
explanation: v²=u²+2as: 0 = 100² + 2a(0.5) → a = −10000 N kg⁻¹ (magnitude 10,000 m/s²). Force = ma = 0.05 kg × 10,000 m/s² = 500 N.

subject: Physics
text: When two objects collide, the force each exerts on the other (by Newton's third law) is:
options: always larger for the heavier/faster object
always equal in magnitude for both objects, regardless of their masses or speeds
zero if one object is at rest
only felt by the lighter object
explanation: By Newton's Third Law, the two colliding objects always exert equal and opposite forces on each other, irrespective of their individual masses or speeds.

subject: Physics
text: Work is said to be done on an object only when:
options: a force is applied to it, regardless of whether it moves
a force causes the object to be displaced in the direction of the force
explanation: Work requires both a force and displacement of the object in the direction of that force; a force with no resulting displacement does zero work.

subject: Physics
text: The energy possessed by a body due to its motion is called:
explanation: Kinetic energy is energy due to motion, given by ½mv²; it is zero when the body is at rest.

subject: Physics
text: Power is best defined as:
options: the total work done by an object
the force applied over a distance
the rate at which work is done
the mass of an object times its velocity
explanation: Power = work done ÷ time taken — it measures how quickly work is performed, not just how much.

subject: Physics
text: A ball thrown straight up momentarily stops at its highest point. At that instant:
options: both its kinetic energy and potential energy are zero
its kinetic energy is zero, but its potential energy is at its maximum for that throw
the force of gravity on it becomes zero
explanation: At the highest point the ball's velocity (and hence kinetic energy) is momentarily zero, while its height — and so potential energy — is at a maximum for that particular throw; gravity still acts on it throughout.

subject: Physics
text: A 50 kg student is lifted straight up 72.5 m in an elevator, then later climbs the stairs to the same height (g = 10 m/s²). How does the gain in potential energy compare between the two methods, and what is its value?
options: Different in each case; climbing stairs gains less potential energy
The same in both cases: 50 × 10 × 72.5 = 36,250 J, since potential energy depends only on height gained, not the path taken
Different: taking the elevator gains more potential energy
Potential energy gained is zero in both cases
explanation: Gravitational PE = mgh depends only on the vertical height change, not the path, so both the elevator ride and the stair climb give the same PE gain: 50 × 10 × 72.5 = 36,250 J.

subject: Physics
text: Simple machines (like pulleys and levers) make work easier mainly by:
options: reducing the total amount of work that needs to be done
changing the magnitude or direction of the force needed to be applied, without reducing total work
eliminating the need for any force at all
explanation: Simple machines change how much force is needed or in which direction it is applied (e.g. a pulley changes direction), but they do not reduce the total work done overall.

subject: Physics
text: A 2 kg ball is thrown up with a velocity of 20 m/s and reaches a maximum height of 19.4 m (g = 10 m/s²). If there were no air resistance, what height would it theoretically reach, and so was any work done by air resistance?
options: Theoretical height (no air resistance) = 20 m; since the actual height (19.4 m) is less, air resistance did negative work on the ball
Theoretical height = 19.4 m exactly, so air resistance did no work
Theoretical height = 40 m; air resistance added energy to the ball
It cannot be determined without the ball's exact shape
explanation: Using v²=u²−2gh with v=0: h = u²/2g = 400/20 = 20 m without air resistance. Since the ball only reached 19.4 m, air resistance removed some kinetic energy, doing negative work on it.

subject: Physics
text: Which of these correctly matches an energy transformation to its example?
options: A solar panel: electrical energy to light energy
Burning of a matchstick: chemical energy to heat and light energy
A glowing electric bulb: light energy to electrical energy
Photosynthesis: heat energy to kinetic energy
explanation: Burning a matchstick converts stored chemical energy into heat and light energy; a solar panel converts light to electrical energy, and a bulb converts electrical energy to light (the reverse of the options given).

subject: Chemistry
text: Who proposed that an atom is a tiny, indivisible, solid sphere?
explanation: Dalton's atomic theory (early 19th century) described atoms as indivisible solid spheres, the earliest atomic model.

subject: Chemistry
text: Thomson's atomic model is popularly known as the:
explanation: Thomson pictured the atom as a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it, like plums in a pudding.

subject: Chemistry
text: In Rutherford's gold foil experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through the foil. What did this show?
options: The atom is a solid sphere
Most of the atom is empty space
explanation: Since most fast-moving alpha particles passed through undeflected, most of the atom's volume must be empty space.

subject: Chemistry
text: A few alpha particles in Rutherford's experiment bounced back at large angles. This indicated that:
options: the positive charge and most mass are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus
explanation: A head-on collision with a small, dense, positively charged nucleus is the only way to deflect a fast alpha particle back at a large angle.

subject: Chemistry
text: What was the main drawback of Rutherford's atomic model?
options: It did not explain why revolving electrons do not lose energy and fall into the nucleus
It said the atom has no nucleus
It placed electrons inside the nucleus
explanation: A charged particle moving in a circular path should continuously radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus — Rutherford's model could not explain why this doesn't happen (atomic instability).

subject: Chemistry
text: According to Bohr's model, electrons revolve around the nucleus:
options: in any path at any distance
in fixed orbits of definite energy, without radiating energy
in a straight line away from the nucleus
explanation: Bohr proposed that electrons occupy only certain fixed-energy orbits (shells) and do not lose energy while revolving in them, which fixed Rutherford's instability problem.

subject: Chemistry
text: The correct historical order of atomic models, earliest to latest, is:
explanation: Dalton (indivisible sphere, early 1800s) → Thomson (plum pudding, 1897) → Rutherford (nuclear model, 1911) → Bohr (fixed orbits, 1913).

subject: Chemistry
text: The atomic number of an element equals the number of:
options: electrons in the outermost shell only
explanation: Atomic number (Z) is defined as the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.

subject: Chemistry
text: Mass number of an atom is the sum of:
explanation: Mass number (A) = number of protons + number of neutrons (together called nucleons).

subject: Chemistry
text: Two atoms have 17 protons each but 18 and 20 neutrons respectively. They are:
explanation: Same atomic number (17, same element) but different mass numbers (35 and 37) makes them isotopes of chlorine.

subject: Chemistry
text: Atom X has 18 protons and 19 neutrons; atom Y has 17 protons and 20 neutrons. X and Y are:
options: isobars (same mass number, different atomic number)
explanation: Mass number of X = 18+19 = 37; mass number of Y = 17+20 = 37 — same mass number but different atomic numbers, so they are isobars.

subject: Chemistry
text: An atom is electrically neutral because:
options: the number of protons equals the number of electrons
neutrons cancel out the protons' charge
explanation: Protons (+1 each) and electrons (–1 each) are equal in number in a neutral atom, so their charges cancel.

subject: Chemistry
text: An atom has atomic number 12 and mass number 24. How many neutrons does it have?
explanation: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 24 − 12 = 12.

subject: Chemistry
text: An atom has 79 protons and a mass number of 197. The number of neutrons in it is:
explanation: Neutrons = mass number − protons = 197 − 79 = 118.

subject: Chemistry
text: An atom has mass number 35 and 18 neutrons. Its atomic number is:
explanation: Atomic number = mass number − neutrons = 35 − 18 = 17 (this is chlorine).

subject: Chemistry
text: The electronic configuration of an atom with atomic number 17 is:
explanation: Shells fill as 2, 8, 8… starting from the innermost (K) shell: 17 electrons distribute as 2 (K) + 8 (L) + 7 (M).

subject: Chemistry
text: The number of valence electrons mainly determines an atom's:
explanation: Valence (outermost shell) electrons are the ones involved in forming bonds, so they decide an element's chemical behaviour and valency.

subject: Chemistry
text: Magnesium has atomic number 12 and mass number 24. Its electronic configuration and number of valence electrons are:
explanation: 12 electrons fill as 2 (K) + 8 (L) + 2 (M); the 2 electrons in the outermost (M) shell are the valence electrons.

subject: Chemistry
text: Atoms of the same element combine to form molecules of:
explanation: When atoms of the same element join (e.g. O2, N2, H2), the result is a molecule of an element, not a compound.

subject: Chemistry
text: Molecules of a compound are formed by:
options: atoms of the same element only
atoms of two or more different elements in a fixed ratio
explanation: A compound's molecule contains atoms of two or more different elements combined in a fixed, definite ratio, e.g. water (H2O).

subject: Chemistry
text: An atom that loses one or more electrons becomes a:
explanation: Losing negatively charged electrons leaves the atom with more protons than electrons, giving it a net positive charge — a cation.

subject: Chemistry
text: An atom that gains electrons becomes a(n):
explanation: Gaining extra electrons gives the atom more negative charge than positive charge, making it a negatively charged ion — an anion.

subject: Chemistry
text: An ionic bond is formed by:
options: sharing of electron pairs between atoms
complete transfer of electrons from one atom to another
explanation: Ionic bonding involves one atom losing electrons (forming a cation) and another gaining them (forming an anion); the oppositely charged ions then attract each other.

subject: Chemistry
text: A covalent bond is formed when two atoms:
options: share one or more pairs of electrons
explanation: In covalent bonding, atoms share electron pairs so each attains a stable (usually octet) outer-shell configuration, e.g. in Cl2 or H2O.

subject: Chemistry
text: An element with 6 electrons in its outermost shell is most likely to form which kind of molecule with another atom of the same element?
options: a diatomic covalent molecule by sharing electrons
explanation: With 6 valence electrons, it needs 2 more for an octet; two such atoms can share electron pairs to form a diatomic covalent molecule (e.g. O2).

subject: Chemistry
text: The valency of an ion is numerically equal to:
options: the number of neutrons in it
explanation: A Ca2+ ion, for instance, has a valency of 2 — the magnitude of the ionic charge directly gives the combining power (valency).

subject: Chemistry
text: The chemical formula of aluminium oxide (Al3+ and O2–) is:
explanation: Charges must balance: 2 Al3+ ions (total +6) combine with 3 O2– ions (total −6), giving the formula Al2O3.

subject: Chemistry
text: The formula unit mass of water, H2O (H = 1u, O = 16u), is:

subject: Chemistry
text: The law of conservation of mass states that in a chemical reaction:
options: mass of reactants is always greater than mass of products
mass of products is always greater than mass of reactants
the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products
mass can be created but not destroyed
explanation: Matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction — the total mass before the reaction equals the total mass after it.

subject: Chemistry
text: Which pair of ions would combine to form an electrically neutral ionic compound with the formula Ca3(PO4)2?
explanation: To balance charge, 3 Ca2+ ions (total +6) combine with 2 PO4³⁻ ions (total −6), giving Ca3(PO4)2.

subject: Chemistry
text: Which of these correctly represents how NH4+ and SO4²⁻ combine?
explanation: Two NH4+ ions (total +2) are needed to balance one SO4²⁻ ion (−2), giving (NH4)2SO4.

subject: Chemistry
text: A molecule of nitrogen gas, N2, contains:
explanation: N2 is a diatomic molecule of the element nitrogen — two nitrogen atoms triple-bonded together.

subject: Chemistry
text: Two elements A (configuration 2,8,5) and B (configuration 2,8,7) combine. The bond and likely compound formed are:
options: covalent; AB with shared electron pairs
explanation: Both A and B are non-metals close to a full octet (need 3 and 1 electrons respectively) — such non-metal/non-metal combinations typically share electrons, forming covalent bonds rather than transferring them completely.

subject: Physics
text: Sound travels as a:
explanation: Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave — particles of the medium vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction the wave travels, and a material medium is required.

subject: Physics
text: Sound cannot travel through:
explanation: Being a mechanical wave, sound needs particles of a medium to vibrate and transfer energy; vacuum has no particles, so sound cannot travel through it.

subject: Physics
text: In a sound wave, a compression is a region of:
explanation: A compression is where particles of the medium are pushed closer together, so density and pressure are momentarily higher than normal.

subject: Physics
text: The number of complete oscillations/compressions passing a point per second is called the wave's:
explanation: Frequency is defined as the number of complete oscillations (or compressions) occurring per second, measured in Hz.

subject: Physics
text: If 20 compressions of a sound wave pass a fixed point in 4 seconds, its frequency is:
explanation: Frequency = number of compressions ÷ time = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 Hz.

subject: Physics
text: The relationship between speed (v), frequency (f) and wavelength (λ) of a wave is:
explanation: Wave speed equals frequency multiplied by wavelength: v = f × λ, a fundamental relation for all periodic waves.

subject: Physics
text: A sound wave has wavelength 3.44 m and travels at 344 m/s. Its time period is:
explanation: Frequency f = v/λ = 344/3.44 = 100 Hz; time period T = 1/f = 1/100 = 0.01 s.

subject: Physics
text: Loudness of a sound depends mainly on its:
explanation: Loudness is determined by the amplitude of the sound wave — larger amplitude (greater vibration) means louder sound.

subject: Physics
text: The pitch (shrillness) of a sound depends mainly on its:
explanation: A higher frequency sound is perceived as a higher-pitched/shriller sound; pitch and frequency are directly related.

subject: Physics
text: An echo is heard distinctly only if the reflected sound reaches the ear after at least:
explanation: The human ear retains a sound sensation for about 0.1 s; the reflected sound must arrive at least 0.1 s after the original for the two to be perceived as distinct (an echo) rather than blending into reverberation.

subject: Physics
text: In a room, reflected sound reaches the ear 0.05 s after the original sound. This will be perceived as:
options: reverberation (persistence of sound), not a distinct echo
explanation: Since 0.05 s is less than the ear's 0.1 s persistence time, the reflected sound merges with the original rather than being heard as a separate echo — this is reverberation.

subject: Physics
text: Sound waves with frequency above the audible range of the human ear (above 20,000 Hz) are called:
explanation: Sound above about 20 kHz, beyond the upper limit of human hearing, is called ultrasonic sound (used in SONAR, medical imaging, etc.).

subject: Physics
text: A SONAR signal travelling at 1,500 m/s in seawater returns as an echo after 6 s. The depth of the seabed below the ship is approximately:
explanation: Total distance travelled (down and back) = speed × time = 1500 × 6 = 9000 m; depth = half of this = 9000/2 = 4500 m.

subject: Physics
text: The lowest frequency a healthy young human ear can normally detect is about:
explanation: The audible range for humans is roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; below 20 Hz is infrasonic, above 20,000 Hz is ultrasonic.

subject: Physics
text: A thunder sound and a lightning flash are produced together far away. The flash is seen before the thunder is heard mainly because:
options: light has a much higher speed than sound
sound has a much higher speed than light
light needs no medium so it is slower
thunder is produced after the flash, not at the same time
explanation: Light travels at about 3×10⁸ m/s, enormously faster than sound (~340 m/s in air), so the flash reaches our eyes almost instantly while the sound takes a noticeable time to arrive.

subject: Biology
text: Reproduction in which offspring are produced from a single parent, without gametes, is called:
explanation: Asexual reproduction involves only one parent and no fusion of gametes, so offspring are genetically identical to the parent.

subject: Biology
text: Offspring produced by asexual reproduction are genetically identical to the parent because:
options: two parents' genetic material is combined
only mitotic (not meiotic) division is involved, so no new combination of genes occurs
gametes fuse to average the genes
explanation: Asexual reproduction (e.g. budding, fragmentation, vegetative propagation) relies on ordinary cell division (mitosis), which copies the parent's genetic material exactly, with no gene-mixing step.

subject: Biology
text: The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower is called:
explanation: Pollination is specifically the transfer of pollen from the male part (anther) to the female part (stigma); fertilisation (fusion of gametes) happens afterward.

subject: Biology
text: Pollination where pollen from one plant reaches the stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species is called:
explanation: Cross-pollination involves pollen transfer between two different plants of the same species, increasing genetic variation compared to self-pollination.

subject: Biology
text: If a flower's anthers are removed before maturity and pollen from a different plant is dusted onto its stigma, which process has been ensured?
explanation: Removing a flower's own anthers rules out self-pollination; applying pollen from another plant of the same species ensures the seeds result from cross-pollination.

subject: Biology
text: The correct sequence of events in sexual reproduction in flowering plants is:
options: Fertilisation → Pollination → Pollen germination → Zygote formation
Pollination → Pollen germination on stigma → Fertilisation → Zygote formation
Zygote formation → Pollination → Fertilisation → Pollen germination
Pollen germination → Zygote formation → Pollination → Fertilisation
explanation: The correct order is: pollination (pollen reaches stigma) → pollen germination on the stigma → fertilisation (fusion of male and female gametes) → zygote formation.

subject: Biology
text: Flowers that bloom at night and are pollinated by nocturnal insects/bats are usually:
options: white or pale in colour, often strongly scented
explanation: Since night-blooming flowers can't rely on bright colours to attract pollinators in the dark, they tend to be white/pale (more visible at night) and often use strong scent instead to attract nocturnal pollinators.

subject: Biology
text: Vegetatively propagated plants (grown from cuttings, grafts etc.) tend to be more vulnerable to disease than sexually reproduced plants because:
options: they are all genetically identical to the parent, so a disease that affects one can affect the whole population
explanation: Since vegetative propagation produces genetically identical clones, a pathogen or stress that affects the parent plant can wipe out the entire genetically uniform population, unlike a genetically diverse, sexually reproduced population where some individuals may resist.

subject: Biology
text: If a plant species reproduced only by self-pollination over many generations, its genetic diversity would:
options: decrease, as there is little mixing of different genetic material
stay exactly the same as a cross-pollinated species
explanation: Self-pollination repeatedly combines genes from the same plant, reducing genetic variation within the population compared to cross-pollination, which introduces genetic material from different individuals.

subject: Biology
text: The male and female gametes in humans are called respectively:
explanation: The male gamete is the sperm and the female gamete is the egg (ovum); their fusion produces a zygote.

subject: Biology
text: Fertilisation in humans normally occurs in the:
explanation: The sperm meets and fertilises the egg in the fallopian tube; the resulting zygote then travels to the uterus to implant.

subject: Biology
text: During pregnancy, the menstrual cycle stops mainly because:
options: the ovaries stop producing hormones permanently
the uterine lining is needed to support and nourish the developing embryo, so it is not shed
explanation: Once fertilisation occurs, the uterine lining (which would otherwise be shed as menstruation) is retained and maintained by hormones to support the implanted embryo, so menstruation pauses throughout pregnancy.

subject: Biology
text: Assertion: The zygote immediately attaches to the uterus wall after fertilisation. Reason: The uterus wall is always prepared to receive the zygote. The correct evaluation is:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true
explanation: A is false — the zygote first undergoes several divisions over a few days while moving through the fallopian tube before it implants in the uterus; it does not attach immediately. R is true in the sense the uterine lining is hormonally prepared (thickened) each cycle to potentially receive an embryo.

subject: Biology
text: Tomato flowers, where stamens cover the stigma and pollination usually happens before the flower opens, are typically:
explanation: Since the stamens surround and pollinate the stigma within the same flower before it even opens, tomato is a classically self-pollinating plant.

subject: Biology
text: In papaya, male and female flowers are usually borne on separate plants. This generally results in:
options: obligate cross-pollination between male and female plants
explanation: Since male and female flowers are on different plants (dioecious), pollen must travel from a male plant's flower to a female plant's flower — this necessarily means cross-pollination.

chapter: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification
subject: Biology
text: The five kingdom classification of living organisms was proposed by:
explanation: R. H. Whittaker (1969) proposed the widely used five-kingdom classification: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.

chapter: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification
subject: Biology
text: Organisms placed in Kingdom Monera are characterised by:
options: the absence of a true nucleus (prokaryotic cells)
explanation: Kingdom Monera consists of prokaryotes (e.g. bacteria), whose cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles.

chapter: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification
subject: Biology
text: An organism that is unicellular, has a true (well-defined) nucleus, and moves using cilia or flagella would most likely be classified under:
explanation: Protista includes unicellular eukaryotes (organisms with a true nucleus) that often move using structures like cilia, flagella or pseudopodia, e.g. Amoeba, Paramecium.

chapter: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification
subject: Biology
text: Fungi are placed in a separate kingdom from plants mainly because fungi:
options: lack chlorophyll and are heterotrophic (often saprophytic/parasitic), unlike autotrophic plants
explanation: Unlike plants, fungi cannot photosynthesise (no chlorophyll); they obtain nutrition by absorbing organic matter from their surroundings — this fundamental nutritional difference places them in their own kingdom.

chapter: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification
subject: Biology
text: Which of these is NOT one of the five kingdoms in Whittaker's classification?
explanation: Viruses are not placed in any of the five kingdoms at all, since they lack cellular organisation — they aren't considered true 'living cells' by this classification scheme.

chapter: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification
subject: Biology
text: Viruses are excluded from the five-kingdom classification mainly because they:
options: lack cellular organisation (no cell structure of their own) and can't reproduce outside a host cell
explanation: Viruses have no cells of their own — they are essentially genetic material wrapped in a protein coat, and they can only replicate by hijacking a host cell's machinery; this acellular nature puts them outside the five-kingdom system, which is built on cellular organisation.

chapter: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification
subject: Biology
text: Bryophytes and pteridophytes both lack flowers and seeds but are classified separately mainly because:
options: bryophytes lack specialised vascular tissue (xylem/phloem) for transport, while pteridophytes have it
explanation: Pteridophytes possess vascular tissue (xylem and phloem) for conducting water and nutrients, which bryophytes (like mosses) lack — this key structural difference separates the two groups despite both lacking seeds/flowers.

chapter: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification
subject: Biology
text: In the classification hierarchy (Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species), which level groups organisms with the MOST features in common?
explanation: As you move down the hierarchy from Kingdom towards Species, each successive group becomes smaller/more specific but shares more features in common; Genus groups very closely related organisms sharing many features, far more than a broad category like Kingdom or Class.

chapter: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification
subject: Biology
text: An insect can be distinguished from an earthworm mainly by the presence of:
options: jointed legs and a segmented body with an exoskeleton
explanation: Insects have jointed legs and a hard exoskeleton, body features that clearly distinguish them from soft-bodied, legless, segmented earthworms.

chapter: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification
subject: Biology
text: Sponges, despite lacking true tissues and organs, are still classified in the animal kingdom because they:
options: have cell walls made of cellulose
are multicellular, heterotrophic organisms with eukaryotic animal-type cells
explanation: Even without true tissues, sponges are multicellular eukaryotes that feed heterotrophically (filtering food particles), which are defining animal-kingdom characteristics, unlike plant or fungal cells.

chapter: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification
subject: Biology
text: A unicellular organism shows photosynthesis in light but switches to heterotrophic feeding in the dark. This behaviour is typical of organisms placed in:
explanation: Certain protists (classic example: Euglena) can photosynthesise when light is available but feed heterotrophically when it is not — this flexible nutrition is a hallmark used to place such organisms in Protista.

chapter: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification
subject: Biology
text: A multicellular organism with well-differentiated tissues, a backbone, and aquatic respiration in its early life stage would most likely belong to:
explanation: A backbone (vertebral column) places the organism among vertebrate animals; aquatic respiration in the early life stage followed by a different mode later is typical of amphibians within Kingdom Animalia.

chapter: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification
subject: Biology
text: If classification were based only on an organism's habitat (e.g. 'lives in water'), a likely scientific problem would be:
options: it would always give the same groups as the five-kingdom system
very different organisms (e.g. fish, water plants, and aquatic bacteria) would be wrongly grouped together, ignoring their fundamental biological differences
it would be more accurate than cellular classification
no organisms could be classified at all
explanation: Habitat alone ignores fundamental biological traits (cell structure, nutrition, body organisation); very unrelated organisms that merely share an environment (e.g. fish, algae, aquatic bacteria) would end up in the same group despite being biologically very different.

chapter: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
subject: General
text: The main source of energy that powers almost all life and processes on Earth is:
explanation: The Sun provides the energy that drives photosynthesis (the base of most food chains), weather, the water cycle, and climate — making it the primary energy source for Earth's systems.

chapter: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
subject: General
text: The continuous cycling of essential nutrients (like carbon, nitrogen) between living organisms and the non-living environment is called a:
explanation: Biogeochemical cycles (carbon cycle, nitrogen cycle, water cycle etc.) describe how essential elements move repeatedly between the biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) components of the environment.

chapter: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
subject: General
text: The main role of biogeochemical cycles in an ecosystem is to:
options: provide food directly to all organisms
recycle essential nutrients between biotic and abiotic components
explanation: These cycles ensure that a finite supply of elements (carbon, nitrogen, etc.) is continuously reused, moving between living things, the atmosphere, water bodies and soil, rather than being used up and lost.

chapter: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
subject: General
text: The phenomenon primarily responsible for the warming of the Earth's surface and lower atmosphere is:
explanation: Certain atmospheric gases (CO2, methane, water vapour etc.) trap outgoing infrared radiation from Earth's surface, warming the atmosphere — this natural process is the greenhouse effect.

chapter: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
subject: General
text: Which of these is classified as a greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming?
explanation: CO2 is a key greenhouse gas — it absorbs and re-radiates infrared heat, unlike N2, O2 and Ar, which are essentially transparent to infrared radiation and don't trap heat this way.

chapter: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
subject: General
text: The envelope of gases surrounding the Earth, which supports life and regulates climate, is called the:
explanation: The atmosphere is the layer of gases (nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide, etc.) surrounding Earth, essential for breathing, weather, and shielding against harmful radiation.

chapter: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
subject: General
text: The zone of the Earth (including land, water, air) where all living organisms exist is called the:
explanation: The biosphere is the global sum of all ecosystems — the relatively thin zone at Earth's surface where life is found, spanning parts of the land, water and air.

chapter: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
subject: General
text: Deforestation on a large scale is likely to disturb the carbon cycle mainly by:
options: increasing the amount of CO2 absorbed by plants
reducing the number of plants available to absorb CO2 through photosynthesis, increasing atmospheric CO2
having no effect on carbon levels
converting all carbon into oxygen instantly
explanation: Plants absorb atmospheric CO2 during photosynthesis; removing large numbers of them (deforestation) reduces this absorption, so more CO2 remains in or is added to the atmosphere, disturbing the natural balance of the carbon cycle.

chapter: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
subject: General
text: Earth's systems (atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere, biosphere) are best described as:
options: interconnected, continuously exchanging energy and matter with one another
explanation: A central idea of 'Earth as a system' is that its major components constantly interact and exchange matter and energy (e.g. water cycling between hydrosphere and atmosphere, carbon cycling between biosphere and atmosphere) — none works in isolation.

chapter: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
subject: General
text: Human activities such as burning fossil fuels mainly disturb Earth's systems by:
options: removing greenhouse gases from the atmosphere entirely
adding extra carbon dioxide to the atmosphere faster than natural cycles can absorb it, enhancing the greenhouse effect
explanation: Burning fossil fuels releases large amounts of CO2 that natural sinks (plants, oceans) cannot fully absorb at the same rate, so atmospheric CO2 accumulates, strengthening the greenhouse effect and driving global warming.

chapter: Earth as a System: Energy, Matter, and Life
subject: General
text: Sustainable use of Earth's resources means:
options: using resources as fast as possible without any limits
using resources in a way that meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
stopping all use of natural resources
explanation: Sustainability balances meeting current human needs with preserving resources and ecological balance so that future generations can also meet their needs — a core idea tied to Earth-systems thinking.
